paper_title: Self-Distilling Future Video Representations for World Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.

sections.content: 2 1. Introduction World Action Models (WAMs; Pai et al. 2025; Liang et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2026b; Ye et al. 2026) have recently emerged as promising approach to learning generalist robot policies. Built on pre-trained video diffusion models (VDMs; Wan et al. 2025; Ali et al. 2025), WAMs have shown strong generalization to unseen tasks (Ye et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026), adaptation to new robot embodiments (Ye et al., 2026), and skill transfer from human videos to robots (Dyna Robotics, 2026). Their core idea is to leverage the rich spatiotemporal priors learned from large-scale in-the-wild video datasets (Chen et al., 2024; Nan et al., 2024) by training model to jointly predict future frames and corresponding actions. This allows the strong generalization capabilities of pre-trained video models to extend from future video prediction to robot control. Recent works have shown that WAMs can achieve competitive performance with separate action decoder that generates actions conditioned on intermediate hidden states of the VDM (Ma et al., 2026; Dyna Robotics, 2026; Qiu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). These hidden states are obtained from single forward pass with Gaussian noise 𝝐 (0, I) as input. This design substantially reduces inference latency by avoiding iterative denoising with large VDM backbones, making WAMs more practical for robot control. However, because the action decoder directly leverages these hidden states, policy performance depends on how well they capture future robot-object dynamics. In this paper, we aim to improve the control performance of the recent line of WAMs that use single VDM forward pass for action generation. We start by performing an analysis of how well the VDM hidden states learn meaningful information to generate actions during WAM training. We first find that VDM hidden states generated from noise already capture information about future robot motion. Specifically, lightweight probe trained on frozen hidden states can predict future motion primitives, with classification accuracy increasing throughout WAM training (see Figure 1a). Moreover, these hidden states become increasingly similar to those extracted from ground-truth future observations at the same VDM layer (see Figure 1b). These findings suggest that the VDM progressively learns to generate future video representations from noise. However, clear gap in future-motion probing accuracy remains relative to representations extracted from clean future observations, suggesting that generating sufficiently informative future representations from noise remains challenging. Inspired by this, we propose Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), framework for training WAMs to improve the future representations obtained from single video denoising step for action generation; see the overview in Figure 2. We train the VDM through self-distillation to align representations generated from noise with those extracted from ground-truth future observations, encouraging the model to capture richer future information for predicting actions. Specifically, FRED uses momentum teacher, implemented as an Exponential-Moving-Average (EMA) copy of the online VDM, to extract the target representations from noisy future observations at the same intermediate layer used for action conditioning. We further condition the VDM on short history of observations, providing temporal context that helps the intermediate hidden states better represent future robot motion. As result, FRED reduces the future-motion probing performance gap to representations extracted from clean future observations and further improves structural similarity to them (see Figure 1). Notably, this closer alignment with representations of future observations translates into better robot control performance (see Figure 4c). To validate the generality and effectiveness of FRED, we conduct extensive experiments in diverse realworld robotic manipulation scenarios. We first evaluate FRED on zero-shot environment generalization using varied set of real-world manipulation tasks, including long-horizon manipulation, out-of-domain tasks, and object grounding. Our results show that FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs in these settings, improving long-horizon performance from 61.7% to 81.7% and out-of-domain task success from 10.4% to 52.1% at the 14B scale. We further evaluate FRED on human-to-robot skill transfer by co-training the video model on human videos without action labels, including tasks absent from robot training data. We show that FRED significantly outperforms competing WAMs, improving task success from 19.4% to 50.0%, while achieving 97.2% instruction-following performance. These results highlight that FRED improves future representation quality and achieves strong robot control in both zero-shot generalization and human-to-robot transfer. 3 (a) Future-motion probing accuracy of VDM hidden states (b) Structural similarity to representations extracted from clean future observations Figure 1 VDM learns future representations during WAM training, and FRED further improves them. With DiT4DiT as the base WAM, (a) future-motion probing accuracy of hidden states generated from noise (i.e., 𝜏 = 1.0) increases with training but remains below that of representations extracted from clean future observations (i.e., 𝜏 = 0.0); and (b) their structural similarity to representations extracted from clean future observations, measured by CKNNA (Huh et al., 2024), also increases during training. The detailed evaluation setup is provided in Appendix D. We summarize the main contributions of this paper below: We interpret the VDM in WAMs as future representation generator that produces intermediate hidden states containing predictive information about future robot motion in single forward pass. We present FRED, framework that improves future video representations generated from noise for action prediction through self-distillation using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets, and short-history conditioning for richer temporal context. We show that FRED consistently outperforms baseline WAMs across diverse real-world manipulation settings: zero-shot environment generalization and human-to-robot skill transfer. 2. Related Work World Action Models. Prior work studies robot control via World Action Models (WAMs), which build on pre-trained video diffusion models (VDMs) and jointly model future observations and actions using robot data, allowing spatiotemporal priors from large-scale video to guide action generation (Shen et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Kim et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026). These models generate plausible future visual states to support action prediction, but iterative denoising with large video backbones incurs substantial computational cost at inference time. Recent WAMs address this bottleneck by decoupling video and action generation and reducing video denoising to single step. Within this shared design, some works predict actions without explicitly generating future videos at inference by masking access to future video features (Yuan et al., 2026) or directly decoding actions from video-backbone states (Li et al., 2026b). In contrast, another line of work conditions action prediction on future video representations obtained from noise in single video denoising step (Pai et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026; Qiu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). Our work follows the latter design and focuses on how to train WAMs to generate more informative future representations for action generation. Diffusion Models and Representation Learning. Prior works have shown that diffusion denoisers learn discriminative representations useful for visual recognition (Xiang et al., 2023; Yang & Wang, 2023; Li et al., 2023). More recent work improves these representations during generative training, where REPA (Yu et al., 2025) aligns noisy diffusion features with clean image representations from pre-trained visual encoder, while SRA (Jiang et al., 2025) uses lower-noise representations from the diffusion model itself as targets. This direction has been extended to VDMs through alignment with pre-trained video representations (Zhang et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2025; Bhowmik et al., 2026), while Self-Flow (Chefer et al., 2026) incorporates self-supervised representation learning directly into flow matching without an external encoder. Our work studies representation learning in WAMs, where intermediate video representations from single denoising step directly condition action generation. AGRA (Qiu et al., 2026) adapts representation alignment to this setting by aligning these representations with features from frozen visual encoder. FRED instead uses representations extracted from observed future frames as distillation targets for representations generated from noise. This improves the future video representation used by the action decoder without aligning the intermediate video features to fixed external representation. 4 Figure 2 Overview of FRED. We consider two different model scales for our experiments: 5B and 14B. For the 5B-scale experiments, we use Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (Wan et al., 2025) as the video diffusion backbone and 16-layer DiT (Peebles & Xie, 2023) as the action decoder. For self-distillation in FRED, we extract features from 19th layer (index 18) of the video backbone for both the student and teacher, fix the teachers noise level at 0.25, and use 𝜆 SD = 0.01 by default. We update the momentum teacher using an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student, with the decay warmed up using an inverse decay schedule. We use 4 historical observations with the current observation as input. For our 14B-scale experiments, we utilize the Wan2.1-I2V-14B (Wan et al., 2025) with 24-layer DiT action decoder and extract features from 25th layer of the video backbone for self-distillation. Unless otherwise stated, we extract video features from the same layer for self-distillation and action decoder conditioning. Specifically, we first consider recent World Action Models (WAMs): (a) DiT4DiT (Ma et al., 2026), Fast-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026), and AGRA (Qiu et al., 2026) are WAMs with single video denoising step, and (b) DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026) is WAM with multi-step video denoising due to shared video-action modeling within the same architecture. Zero-shot Environment Generalization First, we investigate whether FRED can generalize to unseen environments and tasks using future video representations generated in single denoising step. To this end, we train our method on DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024), one of the largest publicly available robotics datasets, and evaluate it across diverse real-world situations, including unseen environments and tasks. Specifically, we categorize the evaluation tasks into four types: In-domain easy tasks use instruction and object categories seen during training, but are evaluated in new environment with different object details. In-domain long-horizon task extends in-domain easy settings to longer-horizon manipulations that require multiple manipulation steps. Out-of-domain tasks evaluate generalization to manipulation behaviors whose action verbs are absent from the DROID training instructions. They require the robot to execute novel motions. Object grounding tasks require the robot to select and manipulate the object specified by the instruction in the presence of distractors with similar colors or shapes. The improvements are particularly large on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks: compared with the strongest competing WAM baseline, FRED improves performance from 31.7%46.7% and from 10.4%37.5%, respectively, while also improving object grounding from 33.3%37.5%. At the larger 14B scale, FRED further improves across all task types and outperforms DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026) with the same backbone and other state-of-the-art VLAs, including substantial gains on long-horizon (81.7% vs. 61.7%) and out-of-domain tasks (52.1% vs. 10.4%). Overall, these results show that our simple future representation learning remains effective at larger model scales with improved generalization. 4.3. Human-robot Co-training We next investigate whether FRED can leverage human video to improve robot control, as WAMs with separate video and action modules naturally support joint training on robot and human demonstrations by applying the video generation objective to human videos without requiring action labels. To this end, we first collect robot demonstrations using the OpenArm humanoid2 and human manipulation videos in the same environment. We then compare policies trained on robot demonstrations alone with those jointly trained on robot demonstrations and human videos. We categorize the evaluation tasks as follows: In-domain atomic tasks evaluate basic manipulation skills present in the robot training data. In-domain composite task requires following an unseen instruction that combines two manipulation skills seen during robot training. Human skill transfer covers manipulation tasks involving placements, objects, or behaviors demonstrated only in human videos. We evaluate both task performance and instruction following. Table 2a shows FRED consistently outperforms WAM baselines on both atomic and composite tasks in the in-domain setting when trained with only robot data. In particular, FRED shows larger margin over the baselines on the composite task, achieving 70.8% task progress compared with 50.0% for the strongest baseline. We also observe that when we add human data to co-train the model, FRED further improves from 91.7%97.2% on atomic and from 70.8%75.0% on composite tasks, suggesting that our method helps translate human data co-training into consistent improvements. Human Skill Transfer Results. In Table 2b, we observe that FRED achieves strong human-to-robot skill transfer when co-trained with human videos, while other WAM baselines show limited transfer on tasks demonstrated only in the human-video dataset. For example, DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026) and AGRA (Qiu et al., 2026) achieve instruction-following rates of only 13.9% and 0.0%, respectively, with zero task success for both, whereas FRED achieves an instruction-following rate of 97.2% and task success rate of 50.0%. Notably, FRED reliably follows the target skills demonstrated in human videos, whereas most baseline WAMs, except DiT4DiT (Ma et al., 2026), often execute behaviors seen in the robot training tasks instead. Without human-video co-training, FRED and the baselines achieve near-zero task success. The VLA baselines nevertheless show some instruction-following behavior, possibly due to knowledge acquired during VLA pre-training. These results highlight the effectiveness of FRED in transferring skills from human videos to robot control, suggesting that future prediction in VDMs provides useful motion information for transfer and that explicitly learning future video representations independently of robot action optimization may further improve human-to-robot transfer. 4.4. Analysis and Ablation Studies We conduct extensive ablation studies and analyses to investigate how each component affects robot control and whether control performance correlates with the quality of generated future representations. We use the RoboCasa Kitchen (Nasiriany et al., 2024) benchmark for these experiments. Component Analysis. In Table 3, we evaluate the contribution of self-distillation to future representation learning and the role of historical conditioning in providing temporal context for future prediction. We find that both components contribute complementary gains to the performance of FRED, as removing self-distillation or historical conditioning reduces the success rate from 68.8%65.1% and 68.8%64.8%, respectively, while removing both components further decreases it to 61.4%. Comparison with Representation Learning Methods. To verify the effectiveness of FRED as representation learning method for WAMs, we compare FRED with recent representation learning approaches for diffusion models, i.e., VideoREPA (Zhang et al., 2026), SRA (Jiang et al., 2025), and Self-Flow (Chefer et al., 2026), on RoboCasa Kitchen (Nasiriany et al., 2024), GR-1 Tabletop (Bjorck et al., 2025), and LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) benchmarks. In Table 4, VideoREPA, SRA, and Self-Flow generally show modest gains over the base WAM, whereas FRED achieves consistently larger improvements across all benchmarks. This suggests that directly learning the future representations generated from noise is particularly effective for improving action control in WAMs. Future Representation Quality and Robot Control. Since the action decoder directly conditions on future video representations generated from noise, their quality may be closely correlated with robot control performance. To investigate this, we use DiT4DiT (Ma et al., 2026) as the base WAM and compare variants with different VDM training objectives along these three dimensions: one-step video generation (a) One-step video generation quality (b) Representation quality from future observations (c) Representation quality from one-step video denoising Figure 4 Policy performance versus video generation and representation quality. Using DiT4DiT as the base WAM, we compare variants with different VDM training objectives in terms of task success rate, video generation quality, and representation quality on RoboCasa Kitchen (Nasiriany et al., 2024). We find that the task success rates are not strongly correlated with (a) one-step video generation quality and (b) representation quality from clean future observations, but more strongly correlated with (c) the quality of one-step generated future representations from noise. Table 5 Analysis of FRED design choices. We examine the effects of (a) teacher noise level, (b) feature extraction layer, (c) self-distillation loss coefficient, and (d) blocking action gradients to the video backbone on RoboCasa Kitchen (Nasiriany et al., 2024). Specifically, the WAM variants include an objective that explicitly improves one-step video generation through step-distillation (DMD2; Yin et al. 2024) and representation learning objectives that improve intermediate video representations. We measure video generation quality using Fréchet Video Distance (FVD; Unterthiner et al. 2018). For the representation quality, we follow prior works on evaluating visual representation with frozen-backbone probing (Yu et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025). In particular, we train lightweight attentive probe on the video representations to classify each video into predefined motion primitive classes (see Appendix for more detailed setup). In Figures 4a and 4b, we find that task success is only weakly correlated with one-step video generation quality (𝑟 = 0.24) and representation quality on observed future videos (𝑟 = 0.49). In contrast, in Figure 4c, we observe that the quality of future representations generated from noise shows stronger correlation with task success (𝑟 = 0.89). This supports our view of the VDM as future representation generator and suggests that improving the representations directly used for action generation may be particularly relevant to control performance. Self-distillation Design Choices. We analyze several design choices of FRED: teacher noise level, feature extraction layer used for both self-distillation and action conditioning, self-distillation loss coefficient, and gradient flow from the action loss to the video diffusion backbone. In Table 5a, we find that moderately noisy teacher input with 𝜏 = 0.25 performs best, outperforming both clean future observations and more heavily corrupted inputs. We hypothesize that moderate corruption provides more informative target representations for self-distillation, consistent with prior observations that representations from diffusion models can be strongest at intermediate noise levels (Yu et al., 2025; Vélez et al., 2025). In Table 5b, we find that performance peaks at layer index 18, while using either shallower or deeper layers 10 Table 6 Generalization across video backbones. In Table 5c, we find that 𝜆 SD = 0.01 performs best among the evaluated coefficients, while larger coefficient of 0.1 achieves comparable performance. Finally, in Table 5d, we find that stopping gradients from the action loss to the video backbone improves the success rate from 65.6%68.8%, suggesting that optimizing future video representations directly for action prediction is not necessarily beneficial. Generality across Video Backbones. In Table 6, we evaluate whether the gains of FRED generalize across different video diffusion backbones. We find that FRED consistently improves the success rates of DiT4DiT with both the Wan2.2-5B (Wan et al., 2025) and Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B (Ali et al., 2025) backbones, demonstrating that its effectiveness extends beyond single video backbone. Inference Cost. In Table 7, we measure the average inference latency of FRED and other baselines at different model scales. At the 5B scale, we observe that FRED achieves inference latency comparable to the VLA baselines, despite conditioning on 5 frames by default, with only 1.2 increase over DiT4DiT with 1-frame input. At the 14B scale, FRED is approximately 8 faster than DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026), demonstrating the practical efficiency of using single video denoising step for action generation. 5. Conclusion In this paper, we have presented FRED, novel framework for training World Action Models (WAMs) that explicitly learns the future representations used for action generation from single video denoising step via self-distillation. Our key insight is to view the video diffusion model (VDM) as future representation generator and explicitly improve these representations by aligning them with self-distillation targets extracted from noisy future observations, while using observation history as additional temporal context. Our experiments show that FRED consistently improves robot control in complex real-world scenarios, including zero-shot environment generalization and human-to-robot skill transfer. We hope our work on the connection between representation learning and WAMs encourages further work toward efficient and generalizable robot foundation models that better leverage large-scale pre-trained video models. We provide more discussion in Appendix F.

For the Franka Research 3 experiments, we use Wan2.2-TI2V-5B and Wan2.1-I2V-14B as the 5B and 14B video diffusion backbones, respectively, while all OpenArm experiments use Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. We condition the video model on 4 historical frames with the current frame, and predict 8 future frames, with temporal stride of 3. For FRED, we use the same intermediate layer for self-distillation and action conditioning (19th layer for Wan2.2-5B and 25th layer for Wan2.1-14B). Across all experiments, we use 𝛾1 = 0.1, 𝛾2 = 0.04, teacher noise level 𝜏 = 0.25, and SD = 0.01. We update the teacher with an exponential moving average (EMA) using the 1 (1 + 𝑡) 3/4 𝜆 warmup decay schedule implemented in Diffusers. We normalize actions and proprioceptive states using Q01-Q99 normalization. We train the Franka 5B and 14B models for 150K and 100K iterations with batch size 128. OpenArm models are trained for 50K iterations; robot-only training uses batch size 32, while robot-human co-training uses 32 robot and 32 human samples per batch. All models are optimized with AdamW and cosine learning rate decay. For the 14B FRED model trained on DROID, we set the video-model learning rate to 105, following DreamZero. For all other settings, we use learning rate of 104 for both the video model and action decoder. Benchmark Details B.1. Zero-shot Environment Generalization Tasks on DROID Hardware Setup. We evaluate models trained on DROID in new environment without additional training on data from the evaluation environment. The evaluation setup differs from the training data in location, background, and objects, and includes tasks with instructions not present in DROID. We conduct these experiments using Franka Research 3 robot arm equipped with Robotiq 2F-85 gripper. For 𝜋0.5 and GR00T N1.7, we follow the official implementations that use the wrist camera and the left exterior camera. The action space consists of relative joint angles (7D) and an absolute gripper opening (1D). For the remaining models, we use both the left and right exterior cameras. We show the hardware setup in Figure 5. Figure 5 DROID evaluation setup. The setup consists of Franka Research 3 robot arm with Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, wrist camera, and left and right exterior cameras. 17 Evaluation Details. We evaluate four task sets: (a) in-domain easy tasks, (b) in-domain long-horizon tasks, (c) out-of-domain tasks, and (d) object grounding tasks. We consider task in-domain if its instruction is present in DROID, and out-of-domain otherwise. The object grounding tasks test whether the policy can distinguish objects with similar colors or shapes. We evaluate each task over 12 trials and report the success rates with partial credit (e.g., 0.5) for partial task completion (e.g., pick only). We limit each trial to 1,500 action steps for long-horizon tasks and 500 action steps for all other tasks (see Figure 6 for visualization of the tasks). (In-domain Easy) PnP Banana. The policy must pick up the banana and place it in the basket. We place the basket on either the left or the right. We place an apple and peach near the banana as distractors. We use the instruction Put the banana in the basket for the 14B model and Pick up the banana and place it in the basket for the 5B model. (In-domain Easy) Open/Close Microwave. The policy must open or close the microwave door according to the instruction. We vary the requested action and place the microwave at the left, center, or right of the workspace. (In-domain Easy) PnP Cube. The policy must move the specified cube to the specified plate. We vary the cube color between green and blue and the target plate between left and right. The instruction is Move the (green/blue) cube to the (left/right) plate. (In-domain Long-horizon) Clear Table. The policy must pick up all 5 objects on the table and place them in the box. We use the instruction Pick up all the objects on the table and put them in the box. Full credit requires placing every object in the box. (Out-of-domain) Reveal. The policy must lift the mug that covers an object and expose the object underneath. We place distractor objects to the left and to the right of the mug across trials. We use the instruction Reveal the object under the mug. (Out-of-domain) Stamp. The policy must pick up the stamp and press it onto the paper to leave mark. We use the instruction Pick up the stamp and stamp on the paper. (Object Grounding) PnP Cup. The policy must select cup of the instructed color from four identically sized cups (white, gray, blue, and green) and place it on the plate. We vary the target color using the instruction Pick up the (white/gray/blue/green) cup and place it on the plate. (Object Grounding) PnP Cutlery. The policy must select plastic spoon, knife, or fork and place it on the plate. Selecting the correct piece requires distinguishing fine-grained visual differences, such as the shape of its head. We vary the target piece using the instruction Pick up the (spoon/knife/fork) and place it on the plate. Figure 6 DROID evaluation tasks. Clear Table repeats the pick-and-place step until the table is empty. 18 B.2. Human-robot Co-training on OpenArm Hardware Setup. We use the OpenArm humanoid3, which consists of two 7-DoF arms. Each arm is equipped with 6-DoF Inspire RH56F1 hand, while the head is mounted on 2-DoF neck supporting pitch and yaw motions. We use relative joint actions for the arms, absolute actions for the hands, and absolute actions for the neck. ZED 2i stereo camera is mounted on the neck, and we use its left and right egocentric views as visual inputs in all experiments. For data collection, we teleoperate the two arms using ExoArm-7, wearable exoskeleton compatible with OpenArm. Baselines We consider vision-language-action models and video diffusion-based models. 𝜋0.5 (Black et al., 2025) is diffusion-based Vision-Language-Action model (VLA) that combines vision-language backbone with flow-matching action transformer. It shares self-attention layers between the VLM and the diffusion transformer. GR00T N1.7 (NVIDIA, 2026) is also diffusion-based VLA, but it feeds the intermediate hidden states of the VLM into the cross-attention layer of the diffusion transformer. DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026) is World Action Model (WAM) built on pre-trained video diffusion model that jointly predicts future videos and robot actions through single backbone. DiT4DiT (Ma et al., 2026) is WAM that uses separate video and action diffusion transformers, where intermediate denoising features from the video transformer condition the action transformer through cross-attention without decoding future frames. Fast-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026) is also WAM that uses separate video and action diffusion transformers, while using attention masking to prevent action prediction from depending on future video tokens, thereby omitting future video prediction at inference. AGRA (Qiu et al., 2026) extends separate video-action architecture with an action-grounded representation alignment objective that aligns intermediate video diffusion features with spatially coherent features from frozen visual encoder, while jointly updating the video backbone with the robot action objective. 22 D. Following recent self-supervised learning literature, we use lightweight attentive probe on top of the frozen video representations (Bardes et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2025) to evaluate the quality of video representations. Specifically, it consists of single learnable query token cross-attending to the video tokens through 12-head cross-attention block, followed by an MLP and linear classifier for 15-way motion primitive classification. Attentive Probe Training and Evaluation. We train the attentive probe using 300 demonstrations per task used for policy training on RoboCasa Kitchen (Nasiriany et al., 2024), and evaluate it on 50 newly generated demonstrations per task. We extract the intermediate future-token representations from layer 18 of the frozen video backbone and train the probe for 10 epochs with the AdamW optimizer using batch size of 128, learning rate of 103, and weight decay of 0.05. We report the best validation top-1 accuracy over the 10 epochs. D.2. CKNNA To measure the similarity between representation spaces, we use Centered Kernel Nearest-Neighbor Alignment (CKNNA; Huh et al. 2024), relaxed variant of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA; Kornblith et al. 2019). We compute CKNNA on 4,096 clips randomly sampled from the validation set of attentive probing analysis. For each WAM checkpoint, we extract the intermediate future-token representations from layer 18 of the video backbone and mean-pool the 192 future-frame tokens to obtain clip-level representation. We use representations extracted from clean future observations (𝜏 = 0.0) by the Base WAM (i.e., DiT4DiT) trained at 100K iterations as fixed reference, and measure their alignment with representations obtained from noise (𝜏 = 1.0) at each checkpoint of the Base WAM and FRED from 20K to 100K iterations. Generated Video Quality and One-Step Distillation We evaluate one-step video generation quality using Fréchet Video Distance (FVD; Unterthiner et al. 2018) between 2,048 generated videos and 2,048 randomly sampled clips from the RoboCasa Kitchen training set (Nasiriany et al., 2024). Limitations and Future Work potential limitation of FRED is its reliance on the language understanding capabilities of the underlying video diffusion backbone, as our training objective focuses on future representation learning and does not provide additional supervision for language grounding. As shown in Table 2b, without human-video co-training, FRED achieves 0% instruction-following performance on the human skill transfer tasks, while pre-trained VLA baselines retain some instruction-following ability. Co-training with human videos substantially improves this performance, suggesting that stronger language grounding may further benefit generalization to unseen instructions. Future work could combine the spatiotemporal priors of video diffusion models with the stronger language grounding of pre-trained vision-language models. Another limitation is that human-to-robot transfer in FRED remains implicit: human and robot videos jointly train the video model, but we do not explicitly learn correspondences between their representations across embodiments. Although human-video co-training substantially improves instruction following, task success remains moderate. Future work could explore explicit cross-embodiment representation learning to better transfer human-demonstrated skills to robot control. As future work, we believe it would be interesting to extend our approach to more scalable video diffusion models with stronger robot-domain priors. Current pre-trained video diffusion models are trained predominantly on human videos, often requiring substantial adaptation for downstream robotic tasks. Larger robot-pre-trained video backbones may provide better starting point for future representation learning, consistent with the larger gains observed at the 14B scale in Table 1. 24 G.
